subtitle: Seven registers, five flags, a 16-bit address bus, and a timing diagram that shows exactly when each signal moves.

arch.body:
Let’s open the lid on the 8085 and meet what lives inside. The chip has an 8-bit ALU and the accumulator A, where results are gathered. There are general registers B, C, D, E, H, L, which can be used as 16-bit pairs BC, DE, HL. The 16-bit program counter and stack pointer keep track of where you are. Add an instruction register and decoder, timing and control, and five flags: Sign, Zero, Auxiliary carry, Parity, Carry.

One handy trick: the HL pair doubles as a memory pointer M. So how many flags does the 8085 have? Five. The figure shows the functional blocks of the chip.
keynotes: The 8085 has an 8-bit ALU, the accumulator A, general registers B, C, D, E, H, L (usable as 16-bit pairs BC, DE, HL), a 16-bit program counter and stack pointer.
It has five flags: Sign, Zero, Auxiliary carry, Parity and Carry.
The HL pair doubles as memory pointer M.

pins.body:
Chip pins are expensive, so the designers did something sneaky that you will appreciate: they made the same eight lines do two jobs. To save pins the low address byte and the data share lines AD0–AD7. During T1 of a machine cycle they carry A0–A7 and the ALE (address latch enable) pulse tells an external 74LS373 latch to capture them; afterwards the same lines carry data. The high byte A8–A15 is on its own pins.

Why is a latch needed? The lines AD0–AD7 carry the low address only briefly (T1), and the latch holds it stable while the lines switch to carrying data. Other pins: control signals RD̅, WR̅, IO/M̅, S0, S1, and the interrupts TRAP, RST7.5, RST6.5, RST5.5 and INTR. ALE tells the external latch that the lines hold an address right now, so capture it.
keynotes: To save pins the low address byte and the data share lines AD0–AD7; during T1 they carry A0–A7 and the ALE pulse tells an external 74LS373 latch to capture them.
The high byte A8–A15 is on its own pins.
Control signals are RD̅, WR̅, IO/M̅, S0 and S1; interrupts are TRAP, RST7.5, RST6.5, RST5.5 and INTR.

iset.body:
What can an 8085 actually do for you? Its instructions fall into five groups. Data transfer (MOV, MVI, LDA, STA, LXI, LDAX, PUSH, POP). Arithmetic (ADD, ADI, SUB, INR, DCR, INX, DAD, DAA). Logic (ANA, ORA, XRA, CMP, rotates). Branch (JMP, conditional jumps, CALL, RET). And machine control (HLT, NOP, EI, DI).

Instructions are 1, 2 or 3 bytes long: opcode only; opcode + 8-bit data; opcode + 16-bit address or data. Look at the machine-code column in the figure. How many bytes is LXI H,2050H? Three: one opcode byte and two address bytes.
keynotes: Instruction groups: data transfer, arithmetic, logic, branch and machine control (HLT, NOP, EI, DI).
Instructions are 1, 2 or 3 bytes: opcode only; opcode + 8-bit data; opcode + 16-bit address or data.
LXI H,2050H is a three-byte instruction.

modes.body: You already know the addressing modes from the previous course; here are the five the 8085 offers. Immediate (MVI B,05H), register (MOV A,B), direct (LDA 2050H), register indirect (MOV A,M, where HL points to the byte), and implied (CMA, RAL act on A). Four of the five are visible in the program above. So MOV A,M uses register indirect addressing.
keynotes: Immediate (MVI B,05H), register (MOV A,B), direct (LDA 2050H), register indirect (MOV A,M) and implied (CMA, RAL).
In register indirect addressing HL points to the byte.

timing.body:
How long does an instruction take? Three nested clocks answer it for you. A T-state is one clock period. A machine cycle (opcode fetch, memory read/write, I/O read/write) takes 3–6 T-states. An instruction cycle is one to five machine cycles.

The opcode fetch is 4 T-states (T1 address out + ALE, T2 RD̅, T3 read, T4 decode). At 3 MHz, T = 1/(3×10⁶) = 0.333 µs, so a 4-T instruction takes 1.33 µs. Take LDA 2050H: 4 machine cycles (opcode fetch, two operand reads, data read), so 4 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 13 T-states. At 3 MHz that is 13 × 0.333 µs ≈ 4.33 µs. Check the timing diagram of the opcode fetch in the figure.
keynotes: A T-state is one clock period; a machine cycle takes 3–6 T-states; an instruction cycle is one to five machine cycles.
The opcode fetch is 4 T-states; at 3 MHz T = 0.333 µs, so a 4-T instruction takes 1.33 µs.
LDA 2050H takes 4 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 13 T-states, about 4.33 µs at 3 MHz.

summary.body:
Two lines to remember.

  • 8085: A, B–L, PC, SP, five flags; 16-bit address, 8-bit data multiplexed with A0–A7.
  • Opcode fetch = 4 T-states; time = T-states / f.
keynotes: The 8085 has A, B–L, PC, SP and five flags, a 16-bit address and 8-bit data multiplexed with A0–A7.
Opcode fetch is 4 T-states and time = T-states / f.
